title: film-pilot-1-real-footage-measurement
universal_lens: Real-footage computer vision pipelines must reconcile temporal disparity, spatial distortion, and motion ambiguity in broadcast video to enable accurate kinematic inference. The mapping from broadcast pixels to physical meters is a time-dependent projective transformation. A static affine approximation fails because the camera undergoes continuous pan and zoom, inducing severe anisotropic scaling errors that amplify pixel-level noise into macroscopic spatial deviations.
gsi_mapping: GSI employs conformal predictive distributions over tracklet associations to quantify uncertainty in velocity estimates derived from sparse, noisy detection data. GSI treats the per-frame homography as a latent variable in a hierarchical Bayesian model. Pixel coordinates are noisy observations; conformal prediction intervals widen dynamically when camera motion exceeds the stability threshold, ensuring measurement uncertainty strictly reflects the underlying geometric degeneracy of the current frame.
gse_mapping: GSE models player state transitions using Bayesian belief updates conditioned on calibrated movement metrics and camera compensation residuals. GSE utilizes these dynamic homographies to maintain a continuously updated state-space representation of the field. As the camera pans, the engine transitions between local coordinate charts, applying motion-aware association to ensure player tracklets remain consistent across non-linear temporal boundaries.

reasoning_traces.think: The fundamental obstruction to extracting rigorous kinematic data from broadcast footage lies in the conflation of intrinsic camera dynamics with extrinsic player motion. When a broadcast camera pans and zooms, the mapping from the two-dimensional image plane to the three-dimensional physical field is not merely non-linear, but explicitly time-dependent. The provided text highlights a critical failure mode: the application of a static, single-frame homography across an entire video clip. Mathematically, this assumes $H_t \approx H_0$ for all $t$, which is demonstrably false under active cinematography. The consequence of this incorrect assumption is anisotropic scaling amplification. Because the camera compresses the depth axis (the y-axis on the screen) significantly more than the lateral axis (the x-axis), the metric scaling factors diverge drastically ($s_y \gg s_x$). In our specific empirical observation, $s_y = 0.0635$ m/px while $s_x = 0.01407$ m/px. This disparity means that any stochastic noise, sensor grain, or sub-pixel localization error inherent to the object detector ($\delta_y$) is magnified by a factor of roughly 4.5 when projected into physical meters. A mere one-pixel jitter in the vertical direction translates to a 4.5-meter phantom displacement in the real world. This is not a software bug; it is a direct manifestation of projective geometry acting upon noisy data. Therefore, Stages 3 through 6 of the pipeline fail not due to algorithmic incompetence, but because they operate on a fundamentally flawed geometric prior. To rectify this, we must abandon global fits and adopt a per-frame (or per-segment) homography estimation, ideally anchored by detected yard lines or stabilized via feature-based ORB/RANSAC pairs. Until the coordinate system itself is dynamically corrected, any derived velocity or acceleration metrics are mathematically meaningless artifacts of the camera operator's framing choices.

Early sports analytics attempted simple affine mappings, assuming static cameras. The realization that broadcast cameras actively manipulate the view frustum necessitated the shift toward dynamic bundle adjustment and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) techniques, now repurposed here for field reconstruction.

The analyst must therefore model the camera operator as an adversarial agent introducing high-frequency, non-isometric distortions into the observational stream, requiring robust, adaptive filtering to extract the true underlying player states.
